pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s this is a categorical, embodied idea: every human body has a small set of basic needs — food (for energy), water (to stay hydrated), sleep (to rest and grow), and exercise (to keep muscles and the heart strong) — and the body signals when a need is unmet (tired without sleep, thirsty without water, hungry without food). The teaching power is in cause-and-effect drawn from the child's OWN experience rather than abstract categories: they already know what being hungry, thirsty, or sleepy feels like, so the lesson names and organises feelings they have. Keep it concrete (real food, a water bottle, jumping to feel the heart) and avoid nutritional detail (food groups, calories) which belongs later. The goal is the durable frame 'my body needs these things, and it tells me when it doesn't have them', which underpins later digestion, diet, and healthy-lifestyle topics.
bestPractices: Anchor each need to a felt bodily signal the child already knows: hungry→food, thirsty→water, sleepy→sleep, and 'do star jumps, feel your heart' for exercise — so the need is recognised from experience, not memorised.
Teach need→consequence as simple cause and effect ('what happens if you don't sleep?'), because the reason a need exists is the whole point for this age.
Use sorting/matching of everyday pictures (a bed, a meal, a water bottle, running) to the four needs to make the categories concrete and active.
Keep it a shared HUMAN (indeed animal) frame — 'every body needs these' — which links gently to animal needs and to the child's care for pets, without adding nutrition detail.
Avoid over-reaching into food groups, hydration science, or sleep cycles; the objective is naming the four needs and why each matters, kept vivid and personal.
keyRepresentations: Four-need picture set (food, water, sleep, exercise) matched to felt signals (hungry, thirsty, sleepy, heart beating)
A 'daily routine' strip showing when each need is met across a child's day
Simple need→consequence pairs ('no water → thirsty', 'no sleep → tired')
The child's own body as evidence — feel your heartbeat speed up after moving
A care-for-a-character scenario where the child provides each need in turn
commonMisconceptions: 'Food and water are the only needs' — forgetting that sleep and exercise are equally basic needs, not optional extras.
'Only some people/athletes need exercise' — missing that movement is a need for every body.
'Needs are just things I like/want' — not distinguishing a want (sweets, toys) from a need the body requires to work.
'You only need to sleep when you're tired' — missing that sleep is a regular requirement for growth and rest.
'Snacks/juice are the same as meals and water' — an early confusion that anticipates the balanced-diet topic.
'These are human-only needs' — not yet seeing that animals share the same basic needs.

learn.summary: For 5–7s, teach the durable frame 'my body needs these things, and it often tells me when it doesn't have them'. The four basic needs — food (energy to move/think/grow), water (hydration), sleep (rest and growth), exercise (strong muscles and heart) — are anchored to bodily feelings the child already knows: hungry, thirsty and sleepy signal that food, water or sleep is needed, while a heart beating faster during and after moving shows the body working when we exercise (it is not a signal that exercise is missing). The key idea is need→consequence as simple cause-and-effect, drawn from the child's own experience rather than abstract categories or nutritional detail. Keep it concrete and personal, and distinguish a need (the body must have it) from a want (sweets, toys we merely enjoy).

activities.title: Look after a character: meet each need
feedback: When the child meets the matching need: 'Yes — it was yawning, so it needed sleep. Now it's bright again!'
When a mismatched action is tried: 'A drink is good, but it's still yawning — what does a yawn tell us it needs?'
Keep it forgiving with no fail-state: 'There's no way to get it wrong — we're just spotting what the body is asking for.'
Link to the child's own body: 'When YOU yawn, what is your body asking for?'
activities.rationale: Acting out need→consequence may make cause-and-effect immediate and playful, and maps onto feelings the child already knows. The soft meters and behaviour animations are one way to show the draining-and-meeting loop concretely; they are a proposed format, not a required one, and efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: Care for a character (e.g. 'Ollie') whose four needs — food, water, sleep, exercise — gently drain over time, shown by soft meters and by the character's behaviour (rubbing its tummy, yawning, flopping, getting fidgety).
Choose an action — give a meal, give a drink, tuck into bed for a nap, go for a run — and watch the character perk up when the matching need is met.
Deliberately try a mismatched action (a drink when the character is sleepy, a nap when it is hungry) and notice it does NOT fix that droop.
Say out loud which signal means which need: 'yawning means it needs sleep', 'rubbing tummy means it needs food'.
activities.intendedInsight: The body has four distinct needs, and in this game each one has its own signal that only the matching action fixes — a drink won't cure sleepiness, a nap won't cure hunger. (Real bodies are a bit messier: feeling tired can sometimes come from being hungry or thirsty too.)

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: the body and its needs
feedback: 'You tapped the eyes — the body needs sleep to rest and grow.'
'What might you feel if you had no water for a long time?' then reveal 'thirsty'.
Prompt naming over recognition: 'Can you tell me the need before you lift the flap?'
activities.rationale: Naming and the felt-signal link are well supported by a reveal picture. As a scaffold it names the needs clearly; a fixed picture names and prompts recognition but does not itself show a need draining and being met, where the cause-effect insight is strongest.
learnerActions: Look at a picture of a child and tap different parts to reveal each need: tummy→food, mouth→water, closed eyes→sleep, legs/heart→exercise.
For each, reveal 'why' the body needs it (food for energy, water for hydration, sleep for rest and growth, exercise for strong muscles and heart).
Lift a flap for 'what happens without it?' to connect each need to its consequence (no water→thirsty, no sleep→tired).
activities.intendedInsight: Each need is tied to a part of the body and a felt signal, and each matters for a specific reason.

activities.title: Sort needs from wants (and match consequences)
feedback: 'Sweets are nice, but does your body stop working without them? What about water?'
'You felt your heart speed up — that's your body working harder when you move.'
If exercise is treated as optional: 'Every body needs to move to keep muscles and the heart strong, not just sports players.'
activities.rationale: Sorting and matching make the categories active and concrete and can teach or check the want-vs-need and 'only athletes exercise' classifications. A sort may teach or check classification but does not by itself elicit the physical experience of meeting and missing needs or the explanation of why a need matters, so it best follows the care activity.
learnerActions: Sort everyday pictures (a bed, a meal, a water bottle, running) into the four needs.
Add a mix of 'want' pictures (sweets, a toy, TV) and decide which are needs the body must have and which are things we simply enjoy.
Match each need to what happens without it ('no sleep → tired', 'no water → thirsty').
Try the heartbeat test: do star jumps, then feel your heart to notice how movement changes the body.
activities.intendedInsight: A need is something the body must have to work; a want is something we like but could do without — and movement is a need for every body, not only for athletes.

activities.title: Advise a tired or hungry character (talk it through)
feedback: 'You told Ollie to have a nap because it was yawning — and why does the body need sleep?' (rest and growth).
If the child names only food and water: 'What about moving? What does exercise do for muscles and the heart?'
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue can elicit the child's reasoning and surface misconceptions. It is a lightweight complement; for this concrete content, acting out need→consequence may be more direct than talk alone, though neither claim is established by the sources.
learnerActions: Talk with a puppet or friendly character who says things like 'Why am I so tired?' or 'Why do I feel so thirsty?'
Advise the character which need to meet and say why (what that need does for the body).
Challenge a mistaken character who says 'I don't need exercise, I just need food and sleep' by explaining what exercise does.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reason aloud about which need is unmet and justify it by naming the need's job (e.g. sleep for rest and growth, exercise for strong muscles and heart).

constraints: Keep content to naming the four needs and why each matters; avoid nutritional detail (food groups, calories, hydration science, sleep cycles) which belongs in later diet and healthy-lifestyle topics.
Anchor needs to felt signals from the child's own experience rather than memorised categories.
Keep a shared human (and animal) frame — 'every body needs these' — linking gently to animal needs and caring for pets, without adding nutrition detail.

A matching/sorting task or reveal picture can name the needs, check recall, and help classify need-vs-want; it may teach or check classification but does not by itself elicit the physical experience of meeting and missing needs that the care activity is designed to support.
Dialogue and care-sim activities are complementary; neither is a required format, and a static picture can still support naming and recognition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Legacy entry asserted the care-sim idea is 'impossible on a static image', that 3D 'adds nothing', and that a quiz 'assesses rather than builds'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits.

The DfE KS1 claim establishes the curriculum topic (needs for survival; importance of exercise and eating the right foods) but does not support any specific teaching method here, so it is not cited against an activity's pedagogical rationale.

The NHS Eatwell source (balanced foods, 6–8 cups of fluid a day) concerns nutrition/hydration detail the pedagogy deliberately defers for this age; it is retained in the row but not used to drive activity content, and no claim here depends on it.

Pedagogy frames food/water/sleep/exercise as the 'four basic needs'; the KS1 curriculum source lists survival needs as water, food and air (not sleep/exercise), and names exercise and eating the right foods as importance points. The four-need framing is a reasonable age-appropriate teaching choice but is broader than the exact curriculum wording and omits air — flagged for review.

The original pedagogy's 'daily routine strip' representation was not reproduced as an activity; it could be added as a when-is-each-need-met sequencing extension if a future author wishes to restore it.

probeDeeper: If you never drank any water, how would your body start to feel? Why?
Which of these does your body truly NEED to work: food, a toy, sleep, sweets? How can you tell which are needs?
Your friend says 'I don't need exercise, I just need food and sleep.' What would you tell them exercise does for the body?
What does food give your body that lets you run around and think?
assess.correctAnswer: Sleep is a real body need, not just boredom-filling: the body uses it to rest and to grow. Without enough sleep you feel tired and can't think, move or grow properly. (Each need has a job — food for energy, water for hydration, exercise for strength — and missing any one causes a bodily effect.)

errorPatterns.pattern: sleep is just boring or 'doing nothing' — the body doesn't really need it
errorPatterns.nextMove: name rest and growth as sleep's jobs and link a missed night to feeling tired and unable to concentrate
errorPatterns.distractor: Sleep is just for when you're bored — your body doesn't really need it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats sleep as optional or as entertainment and names no body job for it

errorPatterns.pattern: food is only to stop you feeling hungry or for fun, not for energy or growth
errorPatterns.nextMove: connect eating to energy for running and thinking, and to the materials the body needs to grow
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot say food gives the body energy to move, think and grow

errorPatterns.pattern: wants are needs — sweets, toys or TV are treated as basic body needs
errorPatterns.nextMove: sort what the body must have to work from what we simply enjoy
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists things the body merely likes among the four basic needs

errorPatterns.pattern: water only matters when you feel thirsty, not as an ongoing need
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish hydration as an ongoing need, and thirst as a late warning sign
errorPatterns.revealedBy: does not treat water as a continuous need the body always requires

responseLevels.gap: Cannot name the four basic needs, or treats needs and wants as the same; sees sleep or food as optional with no body job.
responseLevels.full: Names the four needs, gives the job of each (food→energy to move/think/grow, water→hydration, sleep→rest and growth, exercise→strength), and describes a consequence of a need not being met (tired without sleep, thirsty and unwell without water); can sort a need from a want.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the four needs but cannot say what each one does for the body or what happens if it is missing — e.g. names sleep as a need but still calls it just resting or boredom.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your body needs food, water, sleep and exercise. Someone says: 'Sleep is just boring — I'd be totally fine if I never slept, I just wouldn't be bored.' Is that right? What does your body actually use sleep for, and what would happen to you if you didn't get any?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks sleep is just something boring to fill gives that answer. A child with the real idea names a body job for sleep (rest and growth) and a consequence of missing it (feeling tired, not being able to think or grow).

sources.claim: KS1 pupils should learn the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air); and describe the importance for humans of exercise, eating the right amounts of different types of food, and hygiene.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1, Animals including humans)

sources.claim: Children aged 2 and over should eat a balanced range of foods and stay hydrated; official guidance recommends 6–8 cups/glasses of fluid a day.
